title: Your character
hook: choosing one trait to work on for a year

segments.voice: Yesterday, your charity. Your line: regular giving. Did you do one good deed that cost nothing, and count it? This week you've placed a school, a teacher, a mosque, a circle and a gift. Today, the one thing all of them are for. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

"And lo! thou art of a tremendous nature." That is how Pickthall renders a line in surah al-Qalam, spoken to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Of everything that could have been praised about him, his courage, his leadership, his patience in hard years, the verse praises his nature, his character. Someone once asked his wife Aisha what his character was like. Her answer, as Sahih Muslim records it: his character was the Qur'an. Not a summary of it. The Qur'an, walking around. Today, the end of the week, and the hardest part of practice: choosing one trait to work on for a year.
screen: `A TREMENDOUS NATURE.` → `HIS CHARACTER WAS THE QUR'AN.` → `ONE TRAIT, ONE YEAR.`

segments.voice: First, how much weight the tradition puts on it. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet says the best of you are those with the best character. Of all the measures he could have picked, that is the one in this hadith. Then the week behind you. A school, a teacher, a mosque, a circle, a regular gift: none of these is the goal on its own. They are tools for becoming a certain kind of person. A ruling known by heart and a temper kept on a short leash are supposed to belong to the same life. Next, why one trait. Character is the slow kind of work. Scholars of the inner life, such as al-Ghazali in his Revival of the Religious Sciences, describe treating a bad trait by practicing its opposite, deliberately, over and over, until the opposite starts to come naturally: the impatient person practicing waiting, the stingy one practicing giving. That is hard to do with ten traits at once. It is possible with one. So you pick one: patience, honesty, gentleness in speech, keeping promises, controlling anger. Last, the companion habit. The tradition calls it muhasabah, taking account of yourself. At the end of a day, a short honest look: where did my trait show up today, and where did it slip? No drama, no despair. Just a ledger, kept daily, the way you'd check a garden. One trait, practiced on purpose and checked each night, for a year.
screen: `THE BEST IN CHARACTER.` · `THE WEEK'S TOOLS SERVE ONE GOAL.` · `PRACTICE THE OPPOSITE.` · `MUHASABAH: A DAILY LEDGER.`

segments.voice: The practice: write it down. Before you write, sit. Breathe slowly and let the week settle. Ask one honest question: which trait, if it grew in me this year, would make the people around me breathe easier? Don't choose the one that sounds best. Choose the one your family would choose for you. Let a word come: patience, gentleness, honesty, generosity, calm. Now think of one moment this week where that trait was missing. Don't punish yourself. Just look at it. Then picture the same moment, with the trait present. If you pray, you can ask Allah for help with it in your own words. After the bell, write the trait down where you'll see it every day. The bell holds the time.
Your character. Akhlaq, the habits of the heart that show in how you treat people, worked on one trait at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one trait. Tonight, before sleep, take thirty seconds of muhasabah: where did your trait show up today, and where did it slip? Tomorrow, your family. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Muslims describe good character, akhlaq, as central to the faith, following the hadith that the best of people are those best in character; some choose one trait to work on, and practice muhasabah, a short daily self-accounting, to watch their progress.

original.note: Arabic: character, nature; the word Aisha used for the Prophet's character.

trapdoor: what you thought: character is just your personality, fixed for life.
what it means: habits of the heart that show in how you treat people, and can change one trait at a time.
what a scholar hears: surah al-Qalam's tremendous nature, Aisha's 'his character was the Qur'an', al-Ghazali's practice of the opposite, and daily muhasabah.
